title: Calls claiming your card bought a gun
summary: Quincy, Illinois, police say callers pretending to be a credit card company's fraud team claim your card was used to buy a firearm in another city. The charge never happened, and some people called don't even have a card from that company. The goal is to get personal details or card numbers, and in one case the caller had the person download Signal to talk to a fake FBI agent.
what_to_do: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card to check for any fraud alert. Don't give personal information to someone who called you, and know that the FBI won't contact you through Signal.

sources.name: Quincy Herald-Whig, reporting the Quincy (Ill.) Police Department warning (Nov 13, 2026)

title: Fake FTC websites and FTC impersonators
summary: The FTC says scammers copy its name, logo and page design to build look-alike websites, and contact people by phone, text, email or social media claiming to be FTC agents, sometimes with fake badges. Some tell you to move your money or hand over cash to keep it safe.
what_to_do: Before typing in personal details, check that the site's address ends in .gov, since real FTC sites always do. A real FTC employee will never ask you to move money or hand cash to anyone.

sources.name: FTC: How to spot fake FTC websites and FTC impersonators

title: Calls claiming your child was hurt and needs money
summary: Norman, Oklahoma, police say callers are telling parents their child was in a crash or an assault and was injured, then asking for money for medical care or bail. Someone may come on the line pretending to be the child, blaming an injury for sounding different, and the caller may say police took the child's phone. They push for fast payment by gift card, payment app or wire transfer.
what_to_do: Hang up and call your child yourself, then contact your local police. Never pay with gift cards or give personal details to someone who called you.

sources.name: KOKH Fox 25, reporting the Norman (Okla.) Police Department warning (Nov 12, 2026)
Norman Transcript, reporting the Norman Police Department warning (Nov 12, 2026)

title: Illegal online pharmacies selling unsafe medicine
summary: The Georgia Attorney General's Office warns that some online pharmacies are illegal and may sell counterfeit, expired, unapproved or poorly stored drugs that can harm your health. Warning signs include selling prescription drugs without a valid prescription, prices that look too low, and no checkable U.S. address or licensed pharmacist.
what_to_do: Before ordering, confirm the pharmacy is licensed through your state board of pharmacy and ask a licensed pharmacist if you have questions. Report a suspicious pharmacy to your state attorney general.

sources.name: WSB-TV via Yahoo News, reporting the Georgia Attorney General's Office alert (Nov 12, 2026)

title: Fake charities asking for holiday donations
summary: Graham, North Carolina, police warn that scammers set up fake charities or pose as real ones during the holiday giving season, reaching people by social media, email, text or phone. They use emotional stories, urgent appeals and look-alike fundraising pages, and may ask for gift cards, cryptocurrency or transfers to personal accounts.
what_to_do: Research a charity with a charity rating service before giving, and donate through its official website rather than a link in a message you did not expect. Report a fake charity to your local police or the FTC.

sources.name: WXLV ABC45, reporting the Graham (N.C.) Police Department warning (Nov 12, 2026)

title: Fake rental listings on real estate websites
summary: North Canton, Ohio, police say scammers are posting fake rental listings on well-known real estate websites. Renters are asked to fill out an application with pay stubs and bank records, then to send a security deposit or other payment by bank transfer, which can lead to lost money and identity theft. Police note that a listing on a familiar site is not proof it is real.
what_to_do: Confirm who owns the property and that the person is allowed to rent it before sharing financial documents or paying any deposit. If you shared information or sent money, contact your local police.

sources.name: Cleveland19, reporting the North Canton (Ohio) Police Department warning (Nov 11, 2026)

title: Calls asking church members to buy gift cards
summary: Police in Ripon, Wisconsin, say callers contacted members of a local church and asked them to buy gift cards, claiming the money would help another member with medical needs. The callers then asked for the card details to be read to them over the phone. Members recognized the scam and warned others.
what_to_do: Never read gift card numbers to someone who calls you, and check any request for help directly with your church or the person named, using contact details you already have.

sources.name: WBAY, reporting the Ripon (Wis.) Police Department warning (Nov 11, 2026)

title: Fake VA grant offers sent on social media
summary: The FTC warns that scammers are mining veterans' social media profiles, such as service history, promotion photos and tagged places, then messaging them about grants while claiming to be from the Department of Veterans Affairs. The messages lead to convincing fake sites that ask for a Social Security number or VA account login. Fake profiles using military lingo are also pushing "guaranteed" investment schemes aimed at veterans.
what_to_do: The VA won't message you on social media, so check any benefit offer by going to the VA's official website yourself, and never give your Social Security number or VA login to someone who contacted you. Don't take investment advice from someone you met online.

sources.name: FTC: A Veterans Day reminder on how to spot scams on social media

title: Callers posing as deputies threaten arrest
summary: Sheriff's offices in Montgomery County, Texas, and Hyde County, North Carolina, are warning about callers who pretend to be deputies, say they have legal papers or a warrant, and threaten arrest unless money is sent. Some use a real officer's name or fake the caller ID. Both offices say deputies never demand payment by phone for warrants, bail, missed jury duty or fees.
what_to_do: Hang up, don't send money or gift cards, and call the sheriff's office at a number you look up yourself, not one the caller gives you.

sources.name: KPRC Click2Houston, reporting the Montgomery County (Texas) Sheriff's Office warning (Nov 9, 2026)
WCTI12, reporting the Hyde County (N.C.) Sheriff's Office warning (Nov 10, 2026)

title: Fake jail calls asking for a fee to free a relative
summary: Court officials and the sheriff's office in Boone County, Missouri, say scammers are using public jail rosters to find people in custody, then calling their family and friends while pretending to be jail, police or court staff. The callers say the person can go home on electronic monitoring once an upfront fee for an ankle device is paid, sometimes naming real judges and booking details, and press for quick payment by payment app, cryptocurrency or gift card.
what_to_do: Hang up and check on the person by calling the jail or court at a number you look up yourself. Court officials don't call asking for money and don't accept gift cards, payment apps or wire transfers.

sources.name: KBIA, reporting warnings from Boone County, Mo., court officials and the Boone County Sheriff's Office (Nov 10, 2026)

title: Fake bank calls telling you to hand cash to a courier
summary: Police in Morristown, New Jersey, warn of callers who pose as your bank, claim there is suspicious activity on your account, and tell you to withdraw a large amount of cash and give it to a courier or other person. The calls can be disguised to look like they come from the real bank, and some callers say you are helping with a secret "sting."
what_to_do: No real bank or police department will ask you to withdraw cash and hand it to someone, so hang up and call your bank using the number on the back of your card. Never give a caller your passwords, PINs or one-time codes.

sources.name: WRNJ Radio, reporting the Morristown Police Department warning (Nov 9, 2026)

title: Scams aimed at service members and veterans
summary: New York's attorney general published a guide to scams that target the military community, including people who charge veterans to "help" with VA claims, offers of quick cash in exchange for pension payments, overpriced financing sold per pay period, and fake charities.
what_to_do: Don't pay anyone to help file your first VA claim, and check any benefits message by logging in to your official account directly.

sources.name: New York Attorney General: Scams targeting the military
Yahoo News, reporting the NY Attorney General's new guide (Nov 9, 2026)

title: Callers pressuring employees to use Bitcoin ATMs
summary: Police in Ocean City, Md., say scammers are calling hotels, complimenting staff and offering a "bonus" for settling a supposed balance with cash from the register or safe through a Bitcoin ATM.
what_to_do: Tell staff that the business owner will never ask them to pay a balance with cash from the register or safe through a Bitcoin ATM. Report any such call to police.

sources.name: CoastTV, reporting the Ocean City Police Department warning

title: Fake FBI agents calling from real FBI numbers
summary: FBI Honolulu warned that scammers are posing as FBI, DEA and Secret Service agents and faking the phone numbers of real FBI offices, so calling back the number can still reach the scammer. Victims are threatened with arrest and told to pay. In one case, the scammer used a video call with a background made to look like a federal office.
what_to_do: Hang up, look up the agency's number yourself, and never pay anyone who says they're a government officer, since real agencies don't demand payment by phone, prepaid card, cryptocurrency or courier.

sources.name: Maui Now, reporting the FBI Honolulu warning (Nov 2, 2026)
FBI IC3 Public Service Announcement I-091726-PSA

title: Fake FTC calls threaten to shut off your phone
summary: The FTC warned that callers posing as FTC officials claim a phone number in your name was used for scams in another country and threaten to disconnect your phone. They transfer you to a fake police officer, tell you to keep the call secret, then claim you're under arrest and demand a "security deposit."
what_to_do: Hang up. Real FTC employees never ask for money, threaten to cut off your phone or tell you to keep a call secret. Report the call to the FTC.

sources.name: FTC: The FTC is not calling to deactivate your phone number

title: Fake campaign "investments" and scam PACs
summary: The FBI warned that scammers are using the midterm elections to run fake campaign investment pools, pose as political action committees, sell merchandise that never ships, and send fake voter registration messages. Some use AI-generated voices of candidates.
what_to_do: Donations are never investments. Check a committee on the Federal Election Commission's website before giving, and confirm your registration on the official federal voter registration site.

sources.name: FBI IC3 Public Service Announcement I-101526-3-PSA
